patient.name: Harold Pembridge
patient.setting: Emergency Department (brought in from his care home)
patient.complaint: Two days of a hugely swollen abdomen, crampy pain and no bowel opening or wind
background: Lives in a nursing home in Bromley
Similar milder episode a year ago that settled

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with an elderly, constipated care-home resident, massive tympanic distension and no flatus; the AXR picture decides sigmoid (coffee bean) or caecal (embryo).

points: Two days of a **hugely swollen**, crampy abdomen.
**No stool and no flatus** since yesterday.

steps.lead: Harold ticks every box: **elderly**, **nursing home**, **chronic constipation**. That combination gives a long, floppy sigmoid loop.
A twisted segment means **obstruction**; if the twist strangles the mesenteric vessels, **ischaemia** follows.
Harold has the **large bowel obstruction** picture of sigmoid volvulus: constipation, tympanic distension, tinkling sounds and vomiting.

visual.title: Where Harold's distension is worst
visual.caption: The twisted sigmoid loop rises out of the **left pelvis** and can fill the whole abdomen.

steps.title: Sigmoid vs caecal volvulus
head: Sigmoid
Caecal
rows: Elderly, care home, constipated (most common in adults)
Small bowel obstruction picture, RIF tenderness

steps.lead: Harold's AXR will be the giveaway: a **coffee bean** loop from the pelvis. A comma-shaped loop from the RIF would be **caecal** (embryo sign).

steps.q: What is the biggest immediate danger in Harold's twisted loop?
o: Closed-loop obstruction leading to ischaemia and perforation
steps.r: Volvulus makes a **closed loop**: both ends are blocked, pressure climbs fast, and **ischaemia, perforation and sepsis** follow.

steps.lead: Harold has no peritonism yet, but every hour of twist raises his risk of **perforation**, **ischaemia** and **sepsis**.

steps.text: Fever, constant pain, peritonism or a high lactate in a volvulus stem mean the bowel is **compromised**: that changes the answer to **emergency surgery**.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (abdominal X-ray) or 'most likely finding on AXR' (coffee bean or embryo sign); CT characterises it further.

points: Bloods, VBG with lactate, IV access.

steps.title: Harold's admission bloods
steps.text: **Electrolyte abnormalities** and dehydration from vomiting. A **normal lactate** argues against bowel ischaemia so far.

steps.r: **Abdominal X-ray** shows the coffee bean (sigmoid) or embryo (caecal) sign. Colonoscopy with air would worsen distension.

steps.lead: Harold's AXR shows a huge, inverted-U loop rising from the pelvis to the right upper quadrant: the **coffee bean sign**.

steps.title: Reading Harold's AXR
nodes: Massively dilated loop of large bowel
Points up towards the right upper quadrant
steps.caption: An embryo-shaped loop arising from the **right lower quadrant** would mean caecal volvulus.

steps.lead: If Harold's film were unclear, or ischaemia were suspected, **CT abdomen** would show the twist and the state of the bowel.

visual.title: Harold's lactate
visual.label: Harold 1.6
visual.caption: Normal lactate and no peritonism: Harold is suitable for **endoscopic decompression**, not straight to theatre.

steps.text: Exam rule: **coffee bean = sigmoid**, **embryo = caecal**. Name the sign and you have named the type, and therefore the treatment.
Do not pick **barium enema** or **colonoscopy** to diagnose an acutely obstructed, distended colon: the AXR is the test.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' Sigmoid without peritonism: rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube. Caecal: right hemicolectomy. Peritonism, fever or high lactate: emergency laparotomy.

points: Harold has no peritonism and a normal lactate.
IV fluids and potassium started; NG tube on free drainage.

steps.q: What is first-line for Harold's uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus?
o: Rigid sigmoidoscopy and rectal flatus tube
steps.r: Unruptured sigmoid volvulus: immediate **rigid sigmoidoscopy** and a **rectal flatus tube** untwist and decompress it. Hemicolectomy is for caecal volvulus.

steps.lead: Harold's loop untwists at sigmoidoscopy with a rush of gas and liquid stool; a **flatus tube** is left in to keep it decompressed.

visual.title: Harold after decompression
visual.caption: Rapid fall in girth and pain confirms successful **decompression**.

steps.lead: When the scope fails, the next step is a **percutaneous colostomy tube** to decompress the loop.
Because Harold's volvulus **keeps recurring**, he is offered **resection/fixation** of the sigmoid once optimised.

steps.title: Volvulus management
nodes: Resuscitate: IV fluids, correct electrolytes, NG tube
Peritonism, fever, high lactate? → urgent laparotomy
Caecal: right hemicolectomy (laparotomy if >12 cm or acidosis)

steps.lead: Had Harold arrived with **severe pain, fever and peritonitis**, he would have gone straight for an urgent **midline laparotomy**.

steps.text: Caecal volvulus is **not** treated by sigmoidoscopy: the twist is out of reach. The answer is **right hemicolectomy**.
A caecum **>12 cm** on imaging means impending perforation; with metabolic acidosis or high lactate, it means emergency laparotomy.

science.exam: Science questions ask why a closed-loop obstruction is dangerous, why elderly constipated patients get sigmoid volvulus, or why the X-ray sign looks the way it does.

steps.title: From twist to perforation
nodes: Long, mobile sigmoid on a narrow mesenteric base

steps.lead: Harold's sigmoid has a **long mesentery** but a **narrow attachment**, so it can spin on its own axis like a balloon on a string.
Years of **constipation** and immobility have stretched Harold's sigmoid into a long, **redundant** loop.

steps.q: Why is Harold's obstruction more dangerous than a simple open-loop obstruction?
o: Both ends are blocked so pressure rises and blood supply fails quickly
The small bowel refluxes into it
steps.r: In a **closed loop**, gas and fluid cannot escape either end: pressure rises fast and compresses the vessels, so **ischaemia and perforation** come sooner.

steps.lead: Harold's loop is closed at both ends by the twist, which is why time matters even when he looks well.
The **coffee bean** on Harold's film is the two limbs of his twisted, gas-filled sigmoid, with the **mesenteric fold** as the central line.

steps.text: Same anatomy, same rule: a **mobile segment with a narrow base** twists. That is why a congenitally mobile caecum predisposes to caecal volvulus.

mcq.q: Which type of volvulus is most common in adults?
mcq.r: **Sigmoid volvulus** is the most common in adults.

mcq.q: Which AXR sign is classic for sigmoid volvulus?

o: Right iliac fossa tenderness with a small bowel obstruction picture
mcq.r: Caecal volvulus: **RIF tenderness**, small bowel obstruction-type picture.

mcq.q: Which is a risk factor for sigmoid volvulus?
mcq.r: Chronic constipation, elderly, nursing home resident and congenital malformations.
**AXR**: coffee bean or embryo sign. CT characterises further.

mcq.q: First-line management of uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus?
o: Rigid sigmoidoscopy and rectal flatus tube
mcq.r: Immediate decompression by **rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube**.

o: Right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis
mcq.r: Caecal volvulus: **right hemicolectomy** with primary ileocolic anastomosis.

mcq.q: Which caecal diameter suggests impending perforation?
mcq.r: Caecum **>12 cm**: emergency laparotomy and ileocaecal resection.

mcq.q: Why is a closed-loop obstruction particularly dangerous?
o: Pressure rises rapidly and compromises blood supply
mcq.r: Both ends blocked: **rapid pressure rise**, early ischaemia and perforation.

glossary.Volvulus: Twisting of a segment of bowel around its own mesentery, causing obstruction and possible ischaemia.
glossary.Sigmoid volvulus: Volvulus of the sigmoid colon; the commonest type in adults, typically elderly and constipated.
glossary.Caecal volvulus: Volvulus of a mobile caecum; gives right iliac fossa pain and a small bowel obstruction picture.
glossary.Mesentery: The fold of peritoneum that attaches bowel to the back of the abdomen and carries its blood vessels.
glossary.Redundant: Describes bowel that is longer than normal and forms extra floppy loops.
glossary.Closed-loop obstruction: Obstruction where a segment of bowel is blocked at both ends, so pressure rises fast.
glossary.Coffee bean sign: AXR appearance of sigmoid volvulus: a huge dilated loop with a central dividing line.
glossary.Embryo sign: AXR appearance of caecal volvulus: a comma-shaped dilated loop arising from the right lower quadrant.
glossary.Tympanic: Drum-like, hollow note on percussion, caused by gas-filled bowel.
glossary.Tinkling bowel sounds: High-pitched bowel sounds heard in mechanical bowel obstruction.
glossary.Air-fluid levels: Horizontal lines on an erect film where gas sits above fluid in obstructed bowel.
glossary.Rigid sigmoidoscopy: Examination of the rectum and sigmoid with a straight rigid scope; used to untwist sigmoid volvulus.
glossary.Flatus tube: A soft rectal tube left in after decompression to let gas escape and stop re-twisting.
glossary.Percutaneous colostomy tube: A tube placed through the abdominal wall into the colon to decompress and anchor it.
glossary.Right hemicolectomy: Removal of the caecum, ascending colon and terminal ileum, joining ileum to colon.
glossary.Ileocolic anastomosis: Surgical join between the ileum and the colon after a right hemicolectomy.
glossary.Ileocaecal resection: Removal of the terminal ileum and caecum.
glossary.Laparotomy: Open abdominal surgery through a large incision, usually midline.
glossary.Peritonism: Signs of peritoneal irritation: guarding, rebound tenderness and rigidity.
glossary.Peritonitis: Inflammation of the peritoneum, often from perforated or dead bowel.
glossary.Ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, leading to damage and death if not reversed.
glossary.Perforation: A hole through the full thickness of the bowel wall.
glossary.Lactate: Product of anaerobic metabolism; a high level suggests ischaemic, compromised bowel.
glossary.Metabolic acidosis: Low blood pH from excess acid such as lactate; a sign of dead bowel in volvulus.
glossary.AXR: Abdominal X-ray, the key diagnostic test for volvulus.
glossary.NG tube: Nasogastric tube used to drain the stomach in bowel obstruction.
glossary.Pseudo-obstruction: Massive colonic dilatation without a mechanical blockage, also seen in frail elderly patients.
glossary.Decompression: Releasing trapped gas and fluid from obstructed bowel to reduce pressure.
glossary.Hypokalaemia: Low blood potassium, common after vomiting in bowel obstruction.

technique.stem: An 82 year old woman who lives in a nursing home has a 2 day history of abdominal distension and pain. She has long-standing constipation and has not passed flatus for 24 hours. Her abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic with tinkling bowel sounds. There is no guarding. An abdominal X-ray shows a large dilated loop of bowel arising from the pelvis.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question with an AXR description: match the patient and the film.

clues: large dilated loop of bowel arising from the pelvis
steps.x: Care home + constipation = redundant sigmoid. Absolute constipation and tinkling sounds = mechanical large bowel obstruction. Loop from the pelvis = sigmoid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sigmoid volvulus** (coffee bean sign).

elim: Pseudo-obstruction dilates the whole colon without a single twisted loop.
Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever, not massive distension.
Ischaemic colitis gives bloody diarrhoea.
Toxic megacolon complicates colitis with bloody diarrhoea and systemic toxicity.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: elderly + care home + constipation + huge loop from the pelvis = sigmoid volvulus.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 1 day history of colicky right-sided abdominal pain and vomiting. She has right iliac fossa tenderness. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray shows a large dilated loop of bowel arising from the right lower quadrant.
technique.q: Which is the most likely finding described on this abdominal X-ray?

steps.x: A finding question: which named sign fits this film?

clues: arising from the right lower quadrant
steps.x: RIF tenderness with an obstruction picture and a dilated loop from the RLQ: **caecal volvulus**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Caecal volvulus on AXR = **embryo sign**.

elim: Coffee bean is sigmoid volvulus, arising from the pelvis.
Double bubble is duodenal atresia.
Rigler's sign is perforation.
Thumbprinting is bowel wall oedema in colitis or ischaemia.

steps.x: **C.** Rule: embryo = caecal, coffee bean = sigmoid.

technique.stem: An 88 year old man with dementia and heart failure has sigmoid volvulus. Rigid sigmoidoscopic decompression has failed. He has no guarding or rebound. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. He is judged too frail for major surgery.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
o: Watch and wait with IV fluids

steps.x: Next step after failed first-line treatment.
Sigmoid volvulus, first-line failed, no peritonism, unfit for resection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Second-line: **percutaneous colostomy tube** decompression.

elim: Laxatives cannot untwist a volvulus and may worsen distension.
Waiting leaves a closed loop to become ischaemic.
Right hemicolectomy treats caecal volvulus.
Doing nothing risks ischaemia and perforation.

steps.x: **B.** Rule: scope fails → percutaneous colostomy tube; recurrent or refractory → resection/fixation.

technique.stem: A 79 year old man has sigmoid volvulus. The surgeon explains that, unlike many bowel obstructions, both ends of the twisted segment are blocked, so this needs urgent treatment.
technique.q: Which best explains why this type of obstruction is so dangerous?
o: Loss of fluid into the lumen causing hypovolaemia only
Rapid rise in intraluminal pressure compromising blood supply
Reflux of small bowel contents into the colon

steps.x: A mechanism question about closed-loop obstruction.

clues: both ends of the twisted segment are blocked
steps.x: Both ends blocked = **closed loop**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas and fluid cannot escape, so **pressure rises fast** and compresses the blood supply.

elim: Overgrowth occurs in any stasis and is not the key danger.
Fluid loss occurs in all obstructions; it does not explain early ischaemia.
Faecal impaction is not the mechanism of volvulus.
Reflux describes an incompetent ileocaecal valve, not the closed-loop risk.

steps.x: **D.** Rule: closed loop = rapid pressure rise = early ischaemia and perforation.

practice.stem: An 86 year old man who lives in a care home has a 3 day history of abdominal distension and has not opened his bowels or passed flatus for 2 days. He takes regular senna for chronic constipation. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. His abdomen is grossly distended and tympanic, without guarding.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Elderly care-home resident with chronic constipation and acute massive tympanic distension is sigmoid volvulus. A carcinoma usually gives a longer history of change in bowel habit and weight loss.

steps.x: Diagnosis: who is this, and what is the obstruction?

clues: not opened his bowels or passed flatus
steps.x: Care home + constipation + acute large bowel obstruction picture.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sigmoid volvulus**.

elim: Pseudo-obstruction usually follows surgery or acute illness, with no mechanical cause.
Carcinoma gives a slower history with weight loss and change in bowel habit.
Diverticulitis gives LIF pain and fever.
Small bowel obstruction vomits early with less distension; adhesions or hernia are usual.

steps.x: **D.** Care home + constipation + huge tympanic abdomen = sigmoid volvulus.

practice.stem: A 41 year old woman has a 1 day history of colicky abdominal pain and repeated vomiting. She has right iliac fossa tenderness and mild distension. Her pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray shows a comma-shaped dilated loop arising from the right lower quadrant.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: RIF tenderness, a small bowel obstruction picture and an embryo-shaped loop from the right lower quadrant is caecal volvulus.

steps.x: Diagnosis: read the AXR description.

clues: comma-shaped dilated loop arising from the right lower quadrant
steps.x: Comma-shaped loop from the RLQ = **embryo sign**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Caecal volvulus**.

elim: Appendicitis does not produce a hugely dilated caecal loop.
Crohn's gives chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and strictures.
Intussusception is mainly in infants, with redcurrant jelly stool.
Sigmoid volvulus arises from the pelvis (coffee bean).

steps.x: **B.** Embryo sign = caecal volvulus.

practice.stem: An 80 year old woman in a nursing home has a 2 day history of abdominal distension, vomiting and absolute constipation. Her abdomen is tympanic. A sigmoid volvulus is suspected and an abdominal X-ray is taken.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal X-ray?
practice.e: Sigmoid volvulus gives the coffee bean sign: a twisted, dilated sigmoid loop with a central mesenteric dividing line.

steps.x: A finding question for sigmoid volvulus.
Classic sigmoid volvulus patient.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Coffee bean sign**.

elim: Football sign is massive pneumoperitoneum in infants.
Lead-pipe colon is chronic ulcerative colitis.
A sentinel loop is a local ileus, e.g. pancreatitis.
Thumbprinting is bowel wall oedema.

steps.x: **A.** Sigmoid = coffee bean.

practice.stem: A 78 year old man with Parkinson's disease has a 2 day history of abdominal swelling and has not passed flatus. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 140/84 mmHg. An abdominal X-ray shows a coffee bean sign.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his abdomen?
o: Board-like rigidity with absent bowel sounds
Tender mass in the left iliac fossa
Tympanic distension with tinkling bowel sounds
practice.e: Sigmoid volvulus causes a large bowel obstruction picture: tympanic distension with tinkling bowel sounds. Rigidity would suggest perforation.

steps.x: A finding question: predict the examination of uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus.
Coffee bean = sigmoid volvulus; immobility and constipation are the background.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Obstruction with gas-filled bowel: **tympanic distension, tinkling bowel sounds**.

elim: Rigidity with silent abdomen means perforation/peritonitis, not the typical finding.
Pulsatile expansile mass is an AAA.
Shifting dullness is ascites, which is fluid, not gas.
A tender LIF mass suggests diverticular abscess or tumour.

steps.x: **E.** Volvulus = tympanic, distended, tinkling.

practice.stem: A 76 year old woman has an abdominal X-ray showing a coffee bean sign. She lives in a nursing home and has limited mobility.
practice.q: Which is the most likely predisposing factor for her condition?
practice.e: Chronic constipation creates a redundant, elongated sigmoid colon that twists on its narrow mesentery: the classic predisposition to sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: A cause question: what predisposes to sigmoid volvulus?
Coffee bean = sigmoid volvulus; care home and immobility go with constipation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic constipation**.

elim: Coeliac disease causes malabsorption, not volvulus.
Hiatus hernia is an upper GI problem.
Previous surgery causes adhesional small bowel obstruction.
UC predisposes to toxic megacolon, not volvulus.

steps.x: **A.** Constipation → redundant sigmoid → volvulus.

practice.stem: An 83 year old man is admitted with sigmoid volvulus. Twelve hours later he develops constant severe abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 94/58 mmHg. His abdomen now has guarding and rebound tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most likely explanation for his deterioration?
practice.e: Volvulus is a closed-loop obstruction; fever, peritonism and a high lactate mean the twisted loop is strangulated and ischaemic.

steps.x: A complication question in a known volvulus.
New fever, shock and peritonism in a closed loop.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The loop has become **ischaemic** (strangulated), risking perforation.

elim: C. difficile gives diarrhoea after antibiotics, not new peritonism in hours.
Pneumonia would not cause guarding and rebound.
Hypokalaemia causes ileus, not fever and peritonism.
A UTI does not cause peritonism.

steps.x: **D.** Volvulus + peritonism + high lactate = ischaemic bowel.

practice.stem: An 85 year old woman from a nursing home has a 2 day history of abdominal distension, absolute constipation and vomiting. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg. Her abdomen is tympanic without peritonism.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Suspected volvulus is diagnosed on abdominal X-ray (coffee bean or embryo sign). An erect CXR looks for perforation, which is not suggested here.

steps.x: Initial investigation in suspected large bowel obstruction.
Classic sigmoid volvulus patient, no peritonism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Abdominal X-ray**.

elim: Barium enema is not the first test in acute obstruction.
Colonoscopy insufflates air and is not diagnostic first-line.
Erect CXR looks for free air; there is no peritonism.
Ultrasound is poor with gas-filled bowel.

steps.x: **A.** Volvulus = AXR first.

practice.stem: A 72 year old man has abdominal distension and absolute constipation. An abdominal X-ray shows dilated large bowel, but the radiologist cannot confirm whether there is a twisted loop. He has no peritonism.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: When the AXR is inconclusive, CT abdomen characterises the volvulus and shows ischaemia or other causes.

steps.x: Second-line investigation after an inconclusive AXR.

clues: cannot confirm whether there is a twisted loop
steps.x: AXR inconclusive in suspected volvulus.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT abdomen**.

elim: Ultrasound is limited by bowel gas.
Barium enema is not used acutely for characterisation.
MRI is slow and not used in acute obstruction.
Waiting risks ischaemia in a closed loop.

steps.x: **C.** AXR unclear → CT.

practice.stem: An 81 year old man has sigmoid volvulus confirmed by a coffee bean sign on abdominal X-ray. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 138/82 mmHg. There is no guarding or rebound. Lactate is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Rigid sigmoidoscopy and rectal flatus tube
practice.e: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus is decompressed first by rigid sigmoidoscopy and a rectal flatus tube. Surgery is for failure, recurrence or peritonism.

steps.x: Initial management of uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus.
Sigmoid, no peritonism, no ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rigid sigmoidoscopy and flatus tube**.

elim: Resection is for failed decompression, recurrence or compromise.
Laxatives and enemas do not untwist the bowel.
Colostomy tube is second-line after sigmoidoscopy fails.
Right hemicolectomy treats caecal volvulus.

steps.x: **E.** Sigmoid, stable = scope and flatus tube.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has caecal volvulus confirmed on CT. Her caecum measures 9 cm. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. There is no peritonism and her lactate is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: First-line treatment of caecal volvulus is right hemicolectomy with primary ileocolic anastomosis. Sigmoidoscopy cannot reach the caecum.

steps.x: Management of caecal volvulus.
Caecal volvulus, not yet >12 cm or compromised.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Right hemicolectomy** with primary ileocolic anastomosis.

elim: Colonoscopic decompression is not first-line for caecal volvulus.
Hartmann's is a left-sided resection with an end colostomy.
Sigmoidoscopy treats sigmoid volvulus.
Sigmoid colectomy treats recurrent sigmoid volvulus.

steps.x: **C.** Caecal = right hemicolectomy.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man with sigmoid volvulus has severe constant abdominal pain. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. His abdomen is rigid with rebound tenderness.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Severe pain, fever and peritonitis in volvulus are emergency indications for urgent midline laparotomy; endoscopic decompression is only for uncomplicated cases.

steps.x: Management when the bowel looks compromised.
Volvulus with peritonitis and fever: bowel compromise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent midline laparotomy**.

elim: A colostomy tube cannot deal with dead or perforated bowel.
A flatus tube alone is for uncomplicated decompression.
Waiting is unsafe with peritonitis.
Sigmoidoscopy is contraindicated with peritonism.

steps.x: **E.** Peritonitis + fever = emergency laparotomy.

practice.stem: An 84 year old woman has her second episode of sigmoid volvulus. The surgeon explains that her anatomy makes the sigmoid colon prone to twisting.
practice.q: Which anatomical feature most explains this?
o: Long sigmoid mesentery with a narrow base
practice.e: A long, redundant sigmoid on a long mesentery with a narrow mesenteric base can spin on its axis, causing volvulus.

steps.x: An applied anatomy question.
Recurrent sigmoid volvulus: a mobile, redundant loop.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Long mesentery with a narrow base**.

elim: A fixed retroperitoneal colon cannot twist.
The ileocaecal valve relates to closed-loop large bowel obstruction, not twisting.
A short mesentery limits movement.
Wall thickness does not make bowel twist.

steps.x: **B.** Mobile loop + narrow base = twists.
